generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, you learn a field's conventions by reading its published work a second time, as a writer rather than for content. Read a well-regarded piece again and watch how it is built: how the writer handles claims, how sources are brought in, how each paragraph is shaped, and how far the writer stays in the background. These recurring choices are the conventions, and noticing them lets you write towards them instead of waiting to be told the rules.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students, each handed an unfamiliar journal article and asked to work out how writing is done in that field.

{{learner-a}} reads it once, for content, and reports back what the article found. Asked about its conventions, {{learner-a}} can only say that it was 'formal and quite hard'. The article has been read, but only as information. Its conventions stayed invisible, because {{learner-a}} never looked at how it was made.

{{learner-b}} reads it twice. The second time, {{learner-b}} ignores the findings and watches the writing: the writer rarely appears, claims are hedged and tied to data, each paragraph opens by stating its point, and sources are woven in rather than listed. {{learner-b}} can now name four conventions of the field and write towards them.

Both students read the same article. Only {{learner-b}} read it as a writer, and so could see the conventions {{learner-a}} missed.
generatedProse.summary: Conventions are learned by reading your discipline as a writer: reading well-regarded work a second time for how it is made, noticing what recurs, and writing towards it. You can now explain that way of reading, appraise a piece against the aspects that reveal its conventions, and choose what to notice in an unfamiliar text. The final lesson puts this to work on the hardest convention of all: writing with a critical edge.

check.body: In the worked example, why could {{learner-b}} name the field's conventions when {{learner-a}} could not?
